project_tracker_diagnostic: Biennial/perennial native thistle with pink-purple discoid heads; leaves armed with relatively narrow marginal spines; common in pastures and roadsides across much of Texas.

project_inclusion.learning_reason: Common, conspicuous, or high-value comparison species for Central Texas field ID.

morphology_keys.habit: Erect thistle, usually under about 1 m.
morphology_keys.leaves: Middle/upper leaves typically relatively broad/ovate, broadly sessile or with small clasping auricles, sometimes short-decurrent. Distinguish from very long bull-thistle spiny stem wings, and from narrow tapering/cuneate C. carolinianum leaves.
morphology_keys.heads: Purple to pink discoid heads, solitary or in small groups; no ray florets.
morphology_keys.phyllaries: Involucre around 12–20 mm high (FNA key and UT Austin detailed Texas treatment). Outer/middle phyllaries often carry a narrow whitish, sticky, glutinous medial ridge; UT Austin describes ~2.5–4 mm ridge on sampled phyllaries. A visible pale line need not be sticky in every photo and is not exclusive among Cirsium.
best_field_traits: spiny but not extremely woolly foliage

photo_strategy.selection_logic: Prefer curated taxon photos plus multiple views from one Central Texas/Texas observation.

look_here_first: FIRST turn the head to its SIDE and measure the GREEN SPINY INVOLUCRE, excluding the purple florets: Texas thistle generally has a small involucre about 12–20 mm high, with outer/middle phyllaries having pale, longitudinal sticky (glutinous) RIDGES. SECOND inspect where a MIDDLE or UPPER stem leaf meets the stem: the broadly sessile base may wrap around as short SPINY EARS (auricles), sometimes weakly descending; compare a LONG continuous spiny wing in bull thistle. Horrid thistle has a much bigger 30–50 mm head involucre AND a SEPARATE ring of leaflike spiny bracts hugging each individual head. Do NOT identify by purple color.

comparisons.key_distinctions: C. horridulum has head-associated spiny collar and larger involucre; C. vulgare has upper-leaf blade spines and long winged stems; C. carolinianum has narrow, tapered/cuneate upper leaf bases versus texanum's broadly sessile ovate leaves.
